title: Online social networking sites

paragraphs.text: Since its launch at Harvard University in 2004, Facebook has achieved a membership of over a billion people on every continent. Although adolescents and college students constitute about 40 per cent of users, according to iStrategyLabs in Washington DC, the fastest growing segments on Facebook are users nearing 40 and those pushing 60. Time spent using social networking sites is growing at three times the rate of regular internet usage as a whole, amounting to almost 10 per cent of the many thousands of hours passed online overall. As social networks proliferate, they are altering the way people think about the internet. Old theories about online socializing are falling away, and fresh theories about the psychosocial relevance of social networking are constantly bubbling up.

Logic would have it that abundant social contacts would be a cure for the blues. The truth of the matter, however, is less straightforward. ‘Nearly all the initial studies about people who used the internet for social interaction suggested that they were getting lonelier,’ says University of Chicago social neuroscientist John Cacioppo. Those studies were based on the notion that people used the internet to replace face-to-face interactions and that relationships formed online stayed online. For the users who couldn't get around, that practice seemed to work well, Cacioppo says, but for others it was less satisfactory. A person could not even know for sure who was really on the other end of the line. Psychology studies focused on this scene with critical eyes, often dismissing online socializing as lonely escapism from the disquiet of real relationships.

This view began to change as research grew more nuanced. In a 2008 study at California State University, Los Angeles, psychologists Kaveri Subrahmanyam and Gloria Lin interviewed a total of 192 high school students of different ages, asking them multiple questions about their internet communication strategies, the time they spent online and the sites they frequented. The participants then completed a range of psychological tests. It transpired that neither total time spent online nor time spent communicating online correlated with increased loneliness.

Researchers also study loneliness as a precursor to joining social networks. A 2009 brain-imaging study by Cacioppo showed that the neural mechanisms of lonely and non-lonely people differ according to how they perceive social isolation. While hooked up to a functional MRI machine, the subjects viewed images, some with positive connotations, such as pictures of happy people and money, and others with negative associations, such as scenes of human conflict. As the two groups watched pleasant imagery, the area of the brain that recognizes rewards showed a greater response in non-lonely people. Similarly, the visual cortex of lonely subjects responded more strongly to unpleasant images of people than to unpleasant images of objects, suggesting the attention of lonely people is especially drawn to human distress.

These variations in brain activity hint at why a predisposition to loneliness is such a liability for social networkers. ‘When you're lonely, your brain is in a heightened state of alertness for social threats, even if you're not explicitly looking for them.’ Cacioppo explains. Insults, snubs and gossip all elicit much higher levels of stress in the lonely, measurable in part by elevated production of the stress hormone cortisol. The effect is amplified online because social threats are more difficult to anticipate there. A long silence between replies during an online chat can spawn fears that others are gossiping about you. Another source of insecurity is the very currency of social networks: the number of online ‘friends’. Having a mere handful when others could fill a stadium with theirs can leave lonely individuals feeling their desires are moving even further out of reach.

It is no mystery that social networking sites exert a strong pull like television or video games which deliver instant gratification. Judith Donath, director of the Sociable Media Group at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology's Media Lab, says: ‘Social networking provides a series of mini mental rewards that don't require much effort to receive.’ These rewards serve as jolts of energy that recharge the compulsion engine. Cumulatively, the effect is potent and hard to resist.

Most people will not imperil their psyches if they spend more time networking. For them, two hours a day on Facebook may simply mean two hours less in front of the TV. But for people with a compulsive personality, those hours can grow rapidly, setting off bad consequences at home and even at work. A recent study reported that the most avid Facebook users are spending several hours a day on the site at work, costing those companies whose employees can still access the site 1.5 per cent of office productivity.

Social networking has invaded even more areas of our lives. A dynamic application which is now available is cognitive filtering. This lets users focus on information already vetted by their networks, saving time and aggravation. As you're flipping through movie listings on your smart phone, you might first see starred recommendations from your social network and then details of other films. The danger is that the technology could limit the perspective of its users and breed insular thinking, turning us into a society of myopic clones. Before long, social networking may be part of our every communication tool - changing how we interact and, in the process, changing us.

subtitle: Sites like Facebook and Twitter have evolved into global phenomena in a few years. Whether they are good for our mental health is another matter.
